question: a) Name four objectives of Requirements Engineering
correct_answer:
• Identification and complete collection of requirements: All relevant requirements from stakeholders should be systematically identified and fully recorded to ensure that no important aspects are overlooked.
• Documentation and traceability of requirements: The requirements are documented in a clear, unambiguous and traceable manner so that they are understandable for all participants and traceable throughout the entire project.
• Alignment and consensus-building with stakeholders: A shared understanding and consensus regarding the requirements is established among all stakeholders to avoid misunderstandings and conflicts.
• Management and change control of requirements: Requirements are managed systematically and adapted when necessary, enabling the project to respond to changes among stakeholders or within the project itself and to minimise project risks.
hint: Consider the goals of finding requirements, writing them down clearly, getting everyone to agree, and managing changes over the project lifecycle.

question: b) Name two problems with specifications in natural language.
correct_answer:
• Ambiguity: Requirements formulated in natural language can be interpreted in different ways. Terms or phrases are often not precise, so different people may understand them differently. This leads to misunderstandings and errors in implementation.

• Incompleteness and inconsistencies: Specifications in natural language are often incomplete or contain contradictions. Important details may be missing, or requirements may contradict each other. This results in gaps in system design and makes later adjustments more complex.
hint: Think about the challenges that arise when using human languages, which are naturally flexible and prone to varying interpretations or missing details.

question: c) Why is it important to document requirements in writing? Consider what can happen if requirements are not documented or are documented inadequately.
correct_answer:
• Avoidance of misunderstandings: Written requirements create a shared understanding among all participants. They serve as a reference and help minimize room for interpretation.
• Traceability and transparency: Documented requirements make it possible to track decisions and changes throughout the course of the project. New team members can quickly get up to speed, as the documentation reflects the current state.
• Basis for development and testing: Developers and testers use the documentation as the foundation for their work. They know exactly what needs to be implemented and tested.
• Legal protection: In many projects, the requirements specification is part of the contract. It serves as a legally binding basis for the delivery of services.
hint: Think about how having a written 'single source of truth' helps developers, testers, stakeholders, and legal agreements compared to relying on memory or verbal discussions.

task_title: Task 4.2: Case Study – Health Tracking System
question: a) For each requirement (Req-1 to Req-10), specify the type: F (Functional), Q (Quality), or P (Process).
correct_answer:
Req-1: F (The system should allow users to set and track their daily hydration goals)
Req-2: F (The system should generate monthly health reports)
Req-3: Q (Heart rate data should be encrypted during transmission)
Req-4: Q (Profile picture must be in .jpg format to guarantee compatibility)
Req-5: P (System must comply with GDPR)
Req-6: P (System should store users' health data for at least three years for medical regulations)
Req-7: Q (System should maintain an uptime of 99.9% during peak hours)
Req-8: F (Send motivating message via email/SMS upon workout completion)
Req-9: Q (Allow password reset within 5 minutes)
Req-10: Q (Provide clear and accessible audio/text cues for visually impaired users)
hint: Functional (F) requirements define what the system should do. Quality (Q) requirements specify how well the system performs its functions (e.g., security, usability, reliability). Process (P) requirements constrain how the system is developed or what external regulations it must adhere to.

task_title: Task 4.2: Case Study – Health Tracking System
question: b) Create two user stories based on the case study of the Health Tracking System. Then, review these user stories using the INVEST model.
correct_answer:
User Story 1:
As a user, I want to set and track my daily drinking goals so that I can optimally control my water intake.

User Story 2:
As a visually impaired user, I want to receive clear and accessible feedback during training through text and audio prompts so that I can use the system independently and safely.

INVEST Model Review:
- Independent: Yes, both stories can be implemented independently.
- Negotiable: Yes, details can be coordinated with stakeholders.
- Valuable: Yes, they provide direct value to users.
- Estimable: Yes, the implementation effort can be estimated.
- Small: Yes, the stories are appropriately sized.
- Testable: Yes, clear criteria exist to test both stories (e.g., verifying goal tracking or feedback prompts).
hint: Format your stories using 'As a [user role], I want to [goal] so that [benefit]'. Then, evaluate them against the INVEST principles (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable).

task_title: Task 4.3: Case Study – Smart City Traffic Light Control System

task_title: Task 4.2: Requirements gathering and conflict resolution
question:
During requirements gathering for the Smart City Traffic Light Control System, the following stakeholder conflict has arisen:
"First responders demand that the system enables immediate prioritization of their vehicles to proceed quickly in emergencies. At the same time, pedestrians express concerns that granting priority outside of regular schedules may compromise pedestrian safety."
Assign the appropriate causes from the lecture to the conflicting viewpoints and discuss possible solutions for this conflict.
correct_answer:
Conflict:
- First responders demand immediate prioritization of their vehicles to ensure quick response times.
- Pedestrians fear that unplanned priority for emergency vehicles may compromise pedestrian safety.

Causes:
- Different goals and priorities (efficiency vs. safety)
- Resource conflict (traffic light control cannot simultaneously meet the needs of both groups)
- Safety requirements vs. efficiency requirements
- Stakeholder communication (lack of coordination between groups)
- Stakeholder emotions (safety concerns, urgency)
- Structural factors (technical and organizational framework conditions)

Possible Solutions:
1. Intelligent control: Situation-dependent prioritization, e.g., emergency vehicle priority only when no pedestrians are on the crosswalk.
2. Transparent communication: Make the system's decision logic public to increase acceptance.
3. Technical measures: Additional warning signals (audible/visual) for pedestrians when emergency vehicle priority is activated.
4. Rule-based restrictions: Limit emergency vehicle prioritization through local regulations and safety rules.
5. Adaptive approach: The system can dynamically adjust to the current situation and stakeholder needs.
hint: Analyze the differing goals of the stakeholders (efficiency vs. safety) and propose smart control or communication-based solutions.

task_title: Task 5.1: Fundamentals and Levels of Software Architecture
question: Explain the term "architecture" in general and distinguish it from the understanding of the term in software engineering.
correct_answer: Architecture generally refers to the structured planning and design of systems, such as buildings or organisations. It encompasses physical structures that are determined by the laws of nature. In contrast, in software engineering, "architecture" describes the fundamental structure of a software system: the organisation of components, their interfaces and relationships. It is intangible, dynamic, and significantly more complex, as it is not governed by physical laws but by logical and functional requirements.
hint: Define general architecture in terms of physical structures and physical laws, then contrast it with software architecture's focus on components, interfaces, and logical constraints.

task_title: Task 5.1: Fundamentals and Levels of Software Architecture
question: Why is it important to design and use good architecture for complex software projects?
correct_answer: A good architecture ensures clarity, maintainability, and extensibility of a software system. It facilitates team communication, reduces sources of errors, and enables efficient further development. Especially in complex projects, a well-thought-out architecture is crucial for maintaining quality and stability in the long term.
hint: Think about critical quality attributes like maintainability, scalability, team communication, and long-term project stability.

task_title: Task 5.1: Fundamentals and Levels of Software Architecture
question: How does architecture fit between requirements analysis (RE) and software design?
correct_answer:
Architecture serves as the bridge between requirements analysis (RE) and detailed software design.
Problem space vs. solution space: RE focuses on the problem space (what should be achieved?), while architecture facilitates the transition to the solution space (how will it be structured?).
Abstraction levels: Architecture provides the “big picture”—the overall structure and organization of the system—before software design specifies details such as classes, methods, and processes.
Focus areas: Architecture defines the organization and interaction of components, whereas design determines the functional details and implementation.
hint: Describe architecture as a conceptual bridge, contrasting the 'problem space' (RE) with the 'solution space' (design) and explaining the difference in abstraction levels.

task_title: Task 5.1: Fundamentals and Levels of Software Architecture
question: Explain the significance of the architecture pyramid and its individual levels.
correct_answer:
The architecture pyramid describes the hierarchy of abstraction levels:
Principles and Paradigms:
Fundamental guidelines such as modularity and separation of concerns.
Architectural Styles and Patterns:
Prescribed structures like layered architecture, client-server, and MVC.
Components and Interfaces:
Concrete building blocks of the system and their means of communication.
Implementation: Technical realization in code.
Each level builds upon the previous one and ensures consistency, traceability, and clear orientation throughout the development process.
hint: List and define the four distinct levels of the pyramid, explaining how each level translates abstract principles into concrete code implementation.

question: Explain the term “software component.”
correct_answer: A software component is a self-contained, reusable unit of a software system with a clearly defined purpose. It provides export interfaces for its services and uses import interfaces to integrate other components. Communication occurs via well-defined interfaces, which enables interchangeability and maintainability.
hint: Focus on aspects like self-containment, reusability, and communication via public interfaces (import and export).

question: How can relationships between components be characterized?
correct_answer:
Relationships between components are characterized by interfaces and dependencies. Typical relationships include:
• uses: One component uses the services of another.
• contains: One component includes other components as part of its structure.
Additionally, relationships can be hierarchical, loosely coupled, or tightly coupled, which influences flexibility and maintainability.
hint: Discuss dependencies (like uses and contains) as well as coupling styles (loose vs. tight coupling).

question: Explain what is meant by a Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA).
correct_answer: SOA is an architectural style in which the functionality of a system is provided as loosely coupled, reusable services. These services communicate via standardized interfaces and enable flexible integration and scaling.
hint: Emphasize key principles such as reusable, loosely coupled services communicating via standardized interfaces.

question: Come up with a suitable use case in the context of software engineering where an Agentic Architecture provides added value and describe it. In your description, specifically address the architectural elements of the agentic system used in your use case, as discussed in the lecture.
correct_answer:
Use Case:
A suitable use case for an Agentic Architecture in software engineering is an autonomous DevOps orchestration system for complex, distributed software projects. The goal is the complete automation of build, test, and deployment processes under dynamic conditions (e.g., changing resources, new requirements, outages).

Architectural elements of the agentic system:
• Agents:
- Build Agent: Monitors code commits, initiates builds, and optimizes build pipelines.
- Test Agent: Executes automated tests, prioritizes critical test cases, and reports errors.
- Deployment Agent: Manages rollouts in different environments, considering dependencies and load.
- Monitoring Agent: Analyzes system metrics, detects anomalies, and initiates countermeasures.
- Coordinator Agent: Synchronizes all activities, resolves conflicts, and ensures consistency.
• Sensors/Actuators:
- Sensors: Collect real-time data such as commit frequency, test results, system load, and security warnings.
- Actuators: Perform actions, e.g., automatically scaling resources, triggering rollbacks, or notifying teams.
• Communication Protocols:
- Use of FIPA-ACL for inter-agent communication with performatives such as request, inform, agree.
- Secure, standardized message formats for reliable coordination.
• Coordination & Directory:
- Directory Facilitator: Manages registration and discoverability of all agents.
- Coordinator Agent: Implements a distributed conflict resolution model to avoid deadlocks.
• Coordination Model & Lifecycle Management:
- Each agent follows a defined lifecycle (Initialization → Execution → Termination).
- The system uses a distributed coordination model to ensure scalability and fault tolerance.

Concrete Example:
A developer pushes new code. The Build Agent starts the build, the Test Agent prioritizes security-critical tests. If an error occurs, the Communication Agent informs the team and the Deployment Agent halts the rollout. In parallel, the Monitoring Agent detects increasing system load and initiates automatic scaling. All steps are monitored by sensors and executed by actuators.

Added Value:
• Autonomy & Scalability: Agents act independently and adapt dynamically.
• Efficiency: Automated coordination reduces manual intervention and accelerates release cycles.
• Robustness: Fault tolerance through distributed intelligence and rapid response to anomalies.
• Adaptivity: Learning mechanisms (e.g., reinforcement learning) continuously improve decisions.
• Integration: Seamless interaction with external tools (CI/CD, monitoring, security scanners).

Conclusion:
Agentic Architecture enables a highly adaptive, fault-tolerant, and efficient DevOps system that dynamically adjusts to complex requirements and changing conditions in the software development process.
hint: Develop a concrete scenario (like autonomous DevOps) and outline core agentic concepts: autonomous agents, sensors, actuators, and communication protocols (e.g., FIPA-ACL).

question: Name and briefly describe the three categories of design patterns.
correct_answer:
Creational patterns: Govern the instantiation of objects.
Structural patterns: Describe the composition of classes and objects.
hint: Name the three classical categories (Creational, Structural, Behavioral) and briefly state what aspect of design they manage.

question: Name and briefly explain one pattern for each of the three categories.
correct_answer:
Creational pattern: Singleton – ensures that a class has only one instance.
Structural pattern: Adapter – adapts the interface of a class to another.
Behavioral pattern: Observer – enables notification of multiple objects when the state of a subject changes.
hint: Provide a well-known example of a pattern from each of the creational, structural, and behavioral categories, detailing its purpose.

task_title: Task 6.1: Fundamentals and Definitions of Testing
question: Describe and explain the error hierarchy introduced in the lecture.
correct_answer:
The error hierarchy consists of three levels:
• Error: A human mistake, such as a misunderstanding or a typing error.
• Fault: The defective spot in the code or artefact caused by the error.
• Failure: The visible incorrect behaviour of the system during operation, for example, an incorrect output or a crash.
Connection: Not every error directly results in a failure; only through the fault can an operational failure occur.
hint: Explain the difference and connection between a human mistake (error), its presence in static artifacts (fault), and dynamic incorrect behavior during execution (failure).

task_title: Task 6.1: Fundamentals and Definitions of Testing
question: Explain the essential difference between black-box and white-box tests.
correct_answer:
Black-box test: Tests functionality based on the specification without knowledge of the internal structure. Focus: inputs and outputs.
White-box test: Tests with knowledge of the source code and internal logic. Focus: internal paths, conditions, and control structures.
hint: Contrast testing looking only at inputs/outputs (black-box) with testing the internal logic and control flow of the source code (white-box).

task_title: Task 6.1: Fundamentals and Definitions of Testing
question: Briefly explain the procedure for creating and applying equivalence classes.
correct_answer:
When forming equivalence classes, the input sets are divided into disjoint classes that are considered equivalent for testing purposes. A distinction is made between valid and invalid equivalence classes. For each class, at least one representative test case is selected. The procedure includes:
• Identification of input domains.
• Creation of classes (valid/invalid).
• Selection of representatives for each class.
Goal: Reduce the number of test cases while ensuring high coverage.
hint: Explain partitioning inputs into disjoint domains (valid and invalid), choosing representatives, and how this optimizes test case coverage.

task_title: Task 6.1: Fundamentals and Definitions of Testing
question: What is meant by Test-Driven Development?
correct_answer:
Test-Driven Development (TDD) is an agile development method where:
• Tests are written first as a specification of the requirements.
• The tests initially fail.
• Then, the code is implemented until the tests pass successfully.
• Refactoring is performed to improve the code.
Goals: high test coverage, early error detection, clear specification.
hint: Describe the Red-Green-Refactor workflow, emphasizing writing failing tests prior to implementation.

question: Name possible limitations of equivalence class testing regarding test criteria.
correct_answer:
Error sensitivity: Not all errors are detected, especially with complex dependencies.
Boundary values: May be overlooked if not explicitly tested.
Combinations: Interactions between inputs are often not covered.
Representativeness: A single test case per class does not cover all possible errors.
Economy: Logical errors outside the equivalence classes remain undetected.
hint: Consider the weaknesses of choosing a single representative from a class, including missed boundary errors or non-trivial parameter combinations.

task_title: Task 6.3: White-box Test - Control Flow Graph
question: Develop a control flow graph that represents the method testMe().
correct_answer:
The control flow graph contains the following nodes and edges:
1) Start
2) Initialization of result
3) Loop start (i < a)
4) Condition check ((a > 5 | b > 5) & (c < 10))
5) result = a + b + c (if condition is met)
6) result = result + i
7) Loop end / return to 3
8) return result

The edges connect the nodes according to the sequence in the code.
hint: Map each line of code or structural block (initialization, loop condition, branch checks, body execution) to sequential nodes.

question: Determine specific test inputs (as part of test cases) that can be derived for a branch coverage test. Choose the test cases so that a branch coverage of 100% is achieved.
correct_answer:
Test case 1: a = 2, b = 3, c = 5 (Condition met, loop runs)
Test case 2: a = 0, b = 6, c = 15 (Condition not met, loop skipped)
Test case 3: a = 3, b = 2, c = 12 (Condition not met, loop runs)

With these test cases, all branches in the control flow graph are covered.
hint: Select input parameters that force control flow down every possible edge, ensuring the loop executes, skips, and satisfies both paths of the nested 'if' block.

question: Explain the essential difference between dynamic and static quality assurance, and give 2 examples of each.
correct_answer:
The essential difference is that dynamic quality assurance requires the execution of the program, whereas static quality assurance takes place without executing the program.

Dynamic quality assurance:
• Testing software (e.g. unit tests, integration tests)
• Runtime monitoring (e.g. monitoring, profiling)

Static quality assurance:
• Code reviews
• Static analysis tools (e.g. linters, compiler warnings)
hint: Focus on whether the code is executed (dynamic) or analyzed passively (static) to find defects.

question: Explain the advantages of reviews over tests as discussed in the lecture.
correct_answer:
Reviews offer the following key advantages compared to tests:
• Cost efficiency (Rule of Ten): Since reviews can take place before execution (for example, on requirements or designs), errors are found at a stage where fixing them is still inexpensive. Tests usually detect errors only after they have already been expensively implemented.
• Scope of assessment (Quality attributes): Tests primarily check functional correctness at runtime. In contrast, reviews can also assess static quality characteristics such as maintainability, readability, structure, adherence to coding standards, and documentation.
• Type of error: Reviews directly find the cause (the defect in the code), whereas tests only reveal the symptom (the faulty behavior), which then requires subsequent debugging.
• Knowledge sharing: Reviews also serve as a means of knowledge transfer within the team, as reviewers become familiar with each other's code.
hint: Contrast reviews and tests based on cost of phase-based fixes, ability to inspect non-functional elements, direct symptom resolution, and collaborative team benefits.

question: What disadvantages can you generally imagine reviews have? Name at least two.
correct_answer:
Reviews are often time-consuming and require coordination among several people.
The quality of reviews largely depends on the experience and attention of the reviewers; subjective assessments can lead to inconsistencies.
hint: Consider human factors, such as coordination efforts, subjective bias, time demands, and reliance on reviewer experience.

question: Define the term software measurement and explain its purpose.
correct_answer:
Definition: Software measurement is the systematic assignment of numbers or symbols to attributes of real-world entities (in this context: processes, products, or resources) in order to describe them according to defined rules.

Purpose: The purpose of software measurement is multifaceted and includes:
• Understanding and Evaluation: Establishing an objective assessment of the current state regarding quality and progress.
• Control and Management: Enabling management interventions when measurement values deviate from target values (target-actual comparison).
• Prediction: Estimating future characteristics (e.g., maintenance effort, remaining defects in the system) based on current data.
• Improvement: Identifying weaknesses in processes or products in order to initiate targeted optimization measures.
hint: Explain the mapping of software attributes to numerical systems and highlight how this aids monitoring, decision-making, and structural improvement.

task_title: Task 7.2: Quality Management Principles - Product/Process Objectives
question: Explain to what extent and why you believe this principle makes sense: Product- and process-dependent determination of quality objectives, i.e., the type and intended use of a software system determine the relevant quality characteristics.
correct_answer: The quality objectives must be based on the product and the process, since different types of software (e.g., safety-critical systems vs. web applications) require different quality characteristics. This makes sense because it allows for targeted improvement of the relevant properties.
hint: Argue how varying contexts (such as a medical system vs. an entertainment application) dictate distinct quality targets.

task_title: Task 7.2: Quality Management Principles - Quantitative QM
question: Explain to what extent and why you believe this principle makes sense: Quantitative Quality Management, i.e., target values (quality requirements) and actual values (quality characteristics) must be quantifiable, clearly determinable (objective measures), easy to verify (low measurement effort), and comparable.
correct_answer: Quantitative quality measurement makes sense because it enables objective, verifiable, and comparable statements about quality. This makes progress and deficiencies transparent and understandable.
hint: Highlight how numerical, objective metrics reduce subjectivity and enable transparent monitoring.

task_title: Task 7.2: Quality Management Principles - Constructive QM
question: Explain to what extent and why you believe this principle makes sense: Maximally Constructive Quality Management, i.e., maximize effort for constructive QM in order to optimize analytical QM.
correct_answer:
A high level of effort for constructive measures (e.g., reviews, standards) reduces the effort required for subsequent error analysis and correction.
This makes sense because errors are detected and prevented early on.
hint: Discuss how preventative mechanisms like style guides and design patterns streamline dynamic testing stages.

task_title: Task 7.2: Quality Management Principles - Early Error Detection
question: Explain to what extent and why you believe this principle makes sense: Early Error Detection, i.e., quality assurance activities are especially important in the early phases of a project.
correct_answer:
Explanation: The principle of early error detection states that quality measures should be applied as early as possible in the software lifecycle (e.g., already during requirements analysis or design).

Why does this make sense?
• Cost Explosion (Rule of Ten): The cost of fixing an error increases exponentially depending on the phase in which it is discovered. An error corrected during requirements engineering is many times cheaper than one found only during productive operation (maintenance).
• Avoidance of Subsequent Errors: An error in the design phase often leads to numerous follow-on errors in implementation. Early corrections prevent this chain reaction ("Ripple Effect").
• Planning Certainty: The later errors are found, the more they endanger the schedule and the release date.
hint: Leverage the Rule of Ten and explain how compounding follow-up design errors affect scheduling and final release stability.

question: Explain the concept of 'Integrated Quality Management' (every development activity should consist of a constructive and an analytical component) and why it is sensible.
correct_answer:
Integrated Quality Management, i.e. Every Development Activity Should Consist of a Constructive and an Analytical (Reviewing) Component
Every development activity should include both constructive and analytical elements in order to continuously ensure and check quality. This is sensible, as it allows errors to be detected and corrected at an early stage.
hint: Explain how combining creative development with rigorous review helps find and fix errors early in the lifecycle.

question: Explain the concept of 'Independence of Quality Assurance' (personnel separation between developers and reviewers) and list its benefits.
correct_answer:
Independence of Quality Assurance, i.e. Personnel Separation Between Developers and Reviewers
Optimised Solution:
The personnel separation between developers and reviewers ensures that quality assurance is conducted independently, objectively, and free from conflicts of interest.
This is beneficial because:
• The self-interests of developers (e.g. time constraints, personal preferences) do not influence the review
• The neutrality and credibility of results are increased
• Errors are less likely to be “overlooked” that developers might ignore out of habit or organisational blindness
• Responsibilities are clearly separated, making quality assurance more professional and reliable
hint: Focus on how objectivity, bias reduction, and clear separation of responsibilities are achieved when different people develop and review code.
